network.tdh.impl.metadataDescription: The Rust core, program B, the Python reference, the Lean model and 6529.io, and how they are checked against each other.
network.tdh.impl.title: Implementations
network.tdh.impl.lede: TDH-v1 is one written rule and several programs, written separately from the same text. They are checked against the same test cases and against each other, so a mistake in one shows up as a difference.

network.tdh.impl.backend.conformance: Not a TDH-v1 implementation: the specification lists its 19 deviations and 15 issues, measured by replay and by the daily comparison
network.tdh.impl.written.title: How each was written
network.tdh.impl.written.body: The Python reference came first, written with the specification. Then a separate Rust implementation was written from the specification and the documents it cites, without opening the Python, and it listed every place where it had to guess: 23 in all. P26 now states a rule for each; only the state-read adapter for edition floors stays open.
network.tdh.impl.written.body2: That Rust implementation became the validators’ core without any change to its rules; every copied file is pinned by its hash. Program B was written later, in a separate clean room, from the specifications only. It found that the first version of D131’s netting let steps inside a transaction change TDH. P26 made netting uniform the same day, and vectors 45 to 47 pin its three cases.
network.tdh.impl.lineage.title: Where each implementation came from
network.tdh.impl.lineage.desc: The Python reference was written with P26. The clean-room Rust was written from P26 and the documents it cites, without reading the Python, and became the Rust core with no rule changed. Program B was written from the specifications only, without reading the Rust core, the Python or the clean-room Rust. The Lean model was written from P26. The old backend is replaced by the Rust core at the cutover.
network.tdh.impl.lineage.library: made into a library, no rule changed, hash-pinned

network.tdh.impl.checked.title: How they are checked
network.tdh.impl.checked.vectors.title: Conformance vectors.
network.tdh.impl.checked.vectors.body: 51 small cases, each with the exact values the rule must produce: zero holdings, editions, transfers inside one block, transaction netting, consolidation carry, burns, FirstGM, floors, boost tiers, rounding ties, malformed events, and inputs that must produce no result. Vectors 1 to 18 were derived by hand (18 updated for D131); 19 to 50 were generated by the reference and their derivations checked by hand. Every implementation must pass all of them.
network.tdh.impl.checked.replays.title: Differential replays.
network.tdh.impl.checked.replays.body: Whole days run through more than one implementation and compared with 6529.io’s published values. With D131’s netting, the 2026-10-11 replay reproduces all 10,280 identities and 11,130 wallets; before netting it reproduced 10,278, and the two others were explained (DEV-2).
network.tdh.impl.checked.dual.title: The dual run in every validator.
network.tdh.impl.checked.dual.body: Before it signs, a validator computes TDH with the Rust core and with program B. If they disagree on any value, it does not sign and raises an alarm. Both are built into the validator; the dual run starts when validators run.
network.tdh.impl.checked.daily.title: The daily comparison.
network.tdh.impl.checked.daily.body: From 16 October 2026, 6529 runs the Rust core and the Python reference every day beside 6529.io’s backend and publishes the three results. The Python run reads the Rust run’s own input, after checking its hash, so the two compare computation, not reading Ethereum.
network.tdh.impl.checked.proofs.title: Proofs.
network.tdh.impl.checked.proofs.body: Programs A and B are being built to prove each day’s result from Ethereum’s own history in two different zero-knowledge virtual machines; a minimal Ethereum contract that records proven results is built and tested on a copy of mainnet and is not deployed.
network.tdh.impl.checked.after: After the cutover, 6529.io runs the Rust core itself, so comparing the two no longer tests the computation, only its publication. The independent checks are then the Python reference and program B.

network.tdh.impl.anatomy.title: Inside one vector
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.intro: Vector 18, observed on the 2026-10-11 cycle: one transaction sends a held NextGen token out and back. Its addresses are synthetic. A program reads the transfers and the cycle, and must produce exactly the expected values.
network.tdh.impl.anatomy.derivationBody: Both movements of the token are in one transaction, so the transaction is netted (P26 §7.1): wallet c2’s and wallet c3’s net movements are both zero, and nothing moves. Wallet c2 keeps the acquisition it made 239 days before the snapshot, as 6529.io’s backend does. Before D131, the replay applied both movements and restarted the age at 194 days (DEV-2).
